name: TerarkDB
workload: db_bench with 10 client threads, 20GB requests/thread, 24-byte keys and 2000-byte values; 'heavy_read' (90% read), 'heavy_write' (90% write), fillrandom and fillseq.
claimed_speedup: README table image compare_rocksdb.png (db_bench, TerarkDB vs RocksDB v6.12): QPS heavy_read 695.2K vs 398.1K (~1.75x), heavy_write 215.6K vs 127.1K (~1.70x), fillrandom 204.4K vs 118.8K (~1.72x), fillseq 215.7K vs 208.4K (~1.04x) (ratios derived from page data); P99 read latency heavy_write 73.10us vs 573.68us, P99 write latency heavy_write 75.81us vs 1,029.90us
hardware: Intel(R) Xeon(R) Gold 5218 CPU @ 2.30GHz (2 sockets, 32 cores / 64 threads), 376GB DRAM, NVMe TLC SSD (3.5TB)
tradeoffs: Fork of RocksDB v5.18.3 (data can migrate from RocksDB to TerarkDB but not back); only tested/production-ready on Linux.
caveats: TerarkDB is itself forked from RocksDB v5.18.3 but benchmarked against a newer RocksDB v6.12 (different vintages); results appear only as a table image (compare_rocksdb.png), not in text; exact db_bench command lines, engine options (e.g. whether TerarkZipTable was enabled), compiler and flags are unstated; fillseq gain is only ~1.04x. Latest default-branch commit (2026-05-31) is a README update; last code change 2025-08-25.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "LSM" "benchmark" language:C++ --sort stars

name: Titan (RocksDB plugin)
workload: go-ycsb against TiKV in transaction mode, TiKV-on-Titan vs TiKV-on-RocksDB; 64GB raw dataset with TiKV memory capped at 32GB via cgroup; 16-byte keys, 1KB values (64M keys) and 16KB values (4M keys); data loading, update, point-query, range-iteration and output-size tests.
claimed_speedup: About 70% higher than RocksDB in data-loading (write) scenarios, with the gap growing as value size increases, and 180% higher in update scenarios; also better point-query performance, but underperforms RocksDB on range queries and has slightly higher space amplification
hardware: Intel Xeon E5-2630 v4 (40 cores), 128GB RAM, 1.5TB SATA SSD
stars_or_usage: 514 stars; used as a key-value-separation plugin inside TiKV
tradeoffs: Key-value separation (WiscKey-style) trades range-query performance and space amplification for write/update throughput, especially with large values.
caveats: First-party vendor (PingCAP) blog from 2019 rather than an independent or peer-reviewed source; measured end-to-end through TiKV (writes go through the Raft log first, which the post says dilutes Titan's gain), not Titan vs RocksDB standalone; go-ycsb configs, versions, compiler and flags not stated; percentages read from charts/text with no raw tables.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos "WiscKey" -> tikv/titan; blog post linked from README
